lead: A digital circuit stores and moves only bits. Binary, octal, hexadecimal, 2's complement and BCD are reading rules for the same bit pattern. Binary uses base 2, octal base 8, hex base 16. 2's complement gives negative numbers a single zero and turns subtraction into addition. BCD stores one decimal digit in four bits for displays and clocks. Memory addresses, register maps, sensor readings and embedded control code all use these forms, so converting and checking the range by hand is a daily skill.

blocks.text: Every base-r number is a sum of digit times weight. The weight at position i is r<sup>i</sup>, with i=0 at the rightmost digit. For 1011₂ the weights are 8,4,2,1, so 1011₂ = 8+0+2+1 = 11₁₀. A subscript names the base; r is the radix. Digits run from 0 to r−1. Hex uses A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15.
N = Σ d<sub>i</sub> r<sup>i</sup> from i=0 to n−1
blocks.where: N is the decimal value; d<sub>i</sub> is the digit at position i; r is the base; n is the number of digits.

blocks.text: Decimal to base r uses repeated division. For 45: 45÷2 = 22 remainder 1; 22÷2 = 11 remainder 0; 11÷2 = 5 remainder 1; 5÷2 = 2 remainder 1; 2÷2 = 1 remainder 0; 1÷2 = 0 remainder 1. Read the remainders upward: 101101₂. Pad to 8 bits: 0010 1101.

Binary to octal groups 3 bits, binary to hex groups 4 bits. Start at the decimal point and group outward; pad the outer group with zeros. 101101.01₂ = 101 101 . 010 = 55.2₈. In hex, 0010 1101 . 0100 = 2D.4₁₆.
An n-bit unsigned word holds 0 to 2<sup>n</sup>−1. An 8-bit byte holds 0 to 255. A 4-bit nibble holds 0 to 15.

Sign-magnitude keeps the left bit as sign and the rest as magnitude. It has two zeros, +0 and −0. 1's complement makes a negative by inverting every bit; it also has two zeros. 2's complement makes a negative by inverting every bit and adding 1. It has one zero and needs no separate subtractor.

blocks.where: A and B are n-bit unsigned patterns; B is subtracted by adding its 2's complement; the final carry out of bit n is discarded.

items: Write the n-bit magnitude of the number.
Add 1 and keep only n bits.

blocks.text: For 8 bits, 0100 1110 is 78. Invert: 1011 0001. Add 1: 1011 0010. This pattern is −78. Adding 0010 1101 (45) gives 1101 1111. The carry out is 0. Invert and add 1 to read it: 0010 0001 = 33, so the value is −33.

Signed range for n bits is −2<sup>n−1</sup> to 2<sup>n−1</sup>−1. For 8 bits it is −128 to 127. Overflow occurs when the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out of the sign bit. Overflow is not the same as a carry out of the word.
BCD (binary-coded decimal) stores one decimal digit in four bits, weights 8,4,2,1. 0 to 9 are 0000 to 1001. The six patterns 1010 to 1111 are invalid in BCD.

To add BCD numbers, add each 4-bit nibble as binary. If a nibble sum is greater than 9, or if it produces a carry out, add 0110 (6) to that nibble. Any carry moves to the next nibble. Correct only the nibble that failed; adding 0110 everywhere gives a wrong answer.
Example: 8 + 7. 1000 + 0111 = 1111. 1111 exceeds 9, so add 0110: 1111 + 0110 = 1 0101. The low nibble is 0101 and the carry makes the next nibble 0001, so the answer is 0001 0101, which is BCD 15.
Clocks and seven-segment displays use BCD because each digit is easy to drive.

figure.caption: Adding 8 and 7 in BCD: the low nibble 1111 is above 9, so 0110 is added and the result is 0001 0101 = 15. Only the low nibble needs correction.

spec.title: BCD addition of 8 + 7 with the add-6 correction
spec.aria: Five 8-bit rows show 8 and 7 in BCD, their binary sum 0000 1111, the 0110 correction added to the low nibble, and the final 0001 0101 which is BCD 15.

examples.question: Subtract 45 − 78 in 8-bit 2's complement arithmetic. Then add the BCD numbers 8 and 7, showing the correction.
steps: 2's complement of 78: invert 0100 1110 to 1011 0001; add 1 to get 1011 0010. This is −78 in 8 bits.
Add: 0010 1101 + 1011 0010 = 1101 1111. The carry out of bit 7 is 0.
Read 1101 1111: sign bit is 1. Invert: 0010 0000. Add 1: 0010 0001 = 33. So the value is −33.
1111 is greater than 9, so add 0110 to the low nibble: 1111 + 0110 = 1 0101. Low nibble 0101, carry 1 to next nibble: 0001 0101 = BCD 15.
examples.check:
a = 45
b = 78
print(a - b)
x = 8
y = 7
print(x + y)

traps: Reading a 2's complement pattern as unsigned: 1101 1111 is −33, not 223.
Adding 0110 to every BCD nibble instead of only the nibble above 9 or with carry out.
Grouping hex or octal from the left; group from the decimal point outward and pad the outer group.
Calling a carry out of the word overflow; overflow needs different carries into and out of the sign bit.
Mixing 1's complement (invert only) with 2's complement (invert and add 1).

quiz.q: Why does 2's complement have only one zero?
quiz.a: Inverting 0000 gives 1111; adding 1 gives 0000 with carry out discarded, so no −0 appears.

quiz.q: In 4-bit 2's complement compute 5 − 7. Is there overflow?
quiz.a: 5=0101; −7=1001; sum=1110, which is −2. Carry into and out of the sign bit are both 0, so no overflow.

quiz.q: Why is the final carry thrown away in 2's complement subtraction?
quiz.a: n-bit arithmetic is modulo 2<sup>n</sup>; 2<sup>n</sup>−B represents −B, and the carry out is the 2<sup>n</sup> term outside the n-bit word.

beyond: Not for the exam. Hexadecimal is the usual notation for memory maps, register dumps and colour codes. BCD remains in real-time clocks, energy meters and seven-segment drivers. 2's complement is the integer format in CPUs and DSP chips. Search for “two's complement overflow”, “BCD adder IC” and “hex memory map” to go deeper.
